reasons: [alternatives_counterarguments/major] D1 [C1 mechanisms; C6 assessment and mechanisms; alternatives[1] and [2]; counterarguments[0]; practicalImplications[2]] The draft recommends database-level controls (restricted billing schema and roles) as the main way to comply, but never deals with the strongest objection to that option in a Rails monolith. A single Rails app normally connects to the database with one credential. Schema or role restrictions only separate access if billing code and non-billing code use different database roles, for example through Rails multi-database connections. The supplied coupling data works against the draft here: 214 files reference Billing::, shared tables are 'not yet analysed' (E4), and there are at least 17 invoice jobs. Those unknowns make it hard to say which code should hold the billing role, so they affect the lighter path as well as extraction. The draft treats the coupling unknowns only as an extraction risk (C4, CL11). It presents the lighter path as free of migration risk ('There is no data-migration or cutover risk'). It does not say how 'billing code paths' would be restricted inside a monolith beyond a generic mention of repository controls. The comparison between the options is lopsided as a result.

[reasoning_validity/major] D2 [tradeoffs[3]; counterarguments[3]] The full-time staffing alternative is described inaccurately. tradeoffs[3] says 16 engineer-months 'is still at or below the lower part of past actuals (13 to 18)'. But 16 is above the lowest actual (13) and close to auth's 16.8, so full-time staffing would cover the effort of one of the three reference projects. In calendar terms, 13 engineer-months at 4 FTE is about 3.25 months, which fits January to April. The counterargument response ('within or below') is closer, but it then dismisses the option by citing E10 for 'added headcount does not reliably shorten the schedule'. E10 says nothing about headcount or compressibility. 'Hard to compress' comes from the planner's applicability note, not the source. A decision-relevant lever, more staff, is understated on the basis of a misstatement and unsupported attribution.

[decision_usefulness/major] D3 [verdict; C3 assessment; CL4; CL5; CL6; correctedUserAssumptions[1]] The user asked for an engineer-month figure. The packet's decision objective says to produce 'a defensible range with explicit uncertainty' instead of false precision. The draft gives no effort range for the billing extraction at all. It offers a break-even threshold (an uncalibrated estimate of 3.1 to 4.4 engineer-months would fit capacity, K7/K8) and a conditional (CL5, 'if billing needed effort similar to the past extractions'). The exec still has no figure to put on the table, not even a low-confidence outside-view range such as 'roughly 13 to 18+ engineer-months if billing resembles past extractions, possibly more given ledger and dual-write complexity'. The draft also gives no likelihood (for example 'under 20%') for the deadline question, only 'unlikely'.

[coverage/major] D4 [verdict recommendation; C6; alternatives[1]-[2]; edgeCasesAndFailureModes[3]] The recommended path, lighter controls by the deadline, gets no feasibility assessment against 30 April 2027. The draft admits its effort is unquantified (CL13, C6 weaknesses). Yet it does not apply to that path the yes/no-and-conditions analysis it applies to extraction. Points it leaves out: staffing could be redirected to it; the work components are schema and role refactoring, pgAudit rollout, SoD matrix, CODEOWNERS or deploy controls, and access reviews; and the timeline to meet a possible operating-effectiveness testing period. Today is 11 Nov 2026. If the auditor wants, say, three months of operating evidence, the controls must be live by about the end of January 2027. The draft mentions this only as a generic edge case. The exec is told to switch paths without any check that the new path can make the date.

findings: [minor/reviewer] D1 [verdict; C2 assessment; CL15; correctedUserAssumptions[2]; remainingUncertainty[7]] The figure 'below roughly 1 in 5' for finishing extraction on time (verdict, C2, CL15, correctedUserAssumptions[2]) is new in draft-2 and has no derivation. It is labelled a judgement, but its only support is that none of the three absolute actuals fits in 8 engineer-months (K15). The draft itself calls those actuals 'only a weak proxy' because project sizes are unknown (CL3, C3 mechanisms). It also concedes that billing could be smaller than the past extractions (counterarguments[2]). The number appears to come from review-1's illustrative example ('for example under 20%'), and that example was never meant as a calibrated figure. The draft should say what the threshold rests on, or present it as a qualitative band, so the exec does not read it as a probability.

[minor/reviewer] D2 [furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[1]] furtherResearchThatCouldChangeConclusion[1] says a small inventory 'makes the lighter path comfortably feasible by end of January 2027'. That contradicts the draft's own new material. CL13 and C6 say the effort of the lighter path cannot be quantified. CL18 and K17 say planned staffing supplies only about 2 engineer-months before 31 January unless work starts earlier, and nothing establishes that anyone is available in November or December (E11, E21). Even with a small inventory, pgAudit rollout, SoD matrix, code-ownership and deploy controls and a first access review all remain unestimated. 'Comfortably' overstates the case.

[minor/reviewer] D3 [verdict] The verdict has grown to a very long paragraph. The two answers the exec asked for (the effort range and the yes/no likelihood) are mixed in with the lighter-path conditions and the testing-window caveats, so they are hard to find. One sentence is also garbled: 'a calibrated bottom-up estimate that comes in at about 3.1 to 4.4 engineer-months before calibration'.
